newsitem.title: ISRAEL: High stakes in Israeli-Palestinian poker.
newsitem.headline: High stakes in Israeli-Palestinian poker.

text.p: "There are no winners and no losers if we fight each other." So said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as bloodshed threatened Middle East peace.
He was speaking to Palestinians. The same remark could have been directed by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to Israelis.
After the blood-letting and recriminations about who was responsible, both leaders are assessing what they stand to lose if peace slips through their fingers.
Arafat would be left with nothing if the Oslo accord on Palestinian self-rule crumbled, political analysts on both sides agree.

If violence flared anew and Israel sent in tanks to the autonomous Palestinian areas of the West Bank and Gaza Strip Arafat would probably leave, they said. Israel would again be embroiled in a Palestinian revolt, only this time the other side would have rifles instead of stones.

This doomsday scenario scares PLO officials who have staked all their political capital on Oslo. Arafat, who fled Lebanon after Israel's invasion against his forces there in 1982, sees Oslo as his last chance of laying the foundation stone of his dream, an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza.

Arafat's dream is Netanyahu's nightmare. The right-wing leader, nurtured on revisionist Zionist philosophy, wants to cede only as much land and power to the two million Palestinians under Israel's ultimate control as is necessary to keep them quiet. A sovereign Palestinian state with East Jerusalem is out of the question.
Arafat knows this, but thinks he has no other vehicle for his goals than Oslo, PLO officials say.
Right-wing Israeli analysts agree.
"The basic ingredients have not changed so peacemaking can continue," said Efraim Inbar, of Bar Ilan University's BESA Centre for Strategic Studies.
He said the gunbattles which killed 58 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers had shaken trust between the two peace partners.
"The euphoria of the new Middle East was replaced by the hysteria of the old Middle East," he said. "But it is interest not trust that counts. It is in the interest of both sides to negotiate."
Arafat reflected this on Saturday on his return from the emergency Israeli-PLO summit in Washington, and a swing through sympathetic North African and European states.
"We are giving peace a new chance," he said.

PLO officials said they would probably give peace talks, revived by the White House summit, six months. If implementation of the self-rule agreement signed by Netanyahu's predecessors was still held up the Palestinians would turn to Arab states, urging them to halt normalisation with Israel, the officials said.
The dismantling of the economic and political wall between Israel and the Moslem world was one of the achievements trumpeted by the previous Labour government.

Since the election of Netanyahu, who opposes the land-for-peace foundation of the five-year-old peace process, Arab states have backed off normalisation. Qatar, which a year ago was inching towards trade and political ties, has cooled towards Israel.
Egypt, the first Arab country to make peace with its Jewish neighbour, has been locked in a war of words with Netanyahu for months.

A collapse of Oslo would impair Israel's relations with the European Union, its main trading partner, Western diplomats said. Relations with the United States remain strong. But President Bill Clinton, if re-elected next month, would be in a stronger position to exert pressure on Israel if his administration's long-nurtured peace drive appeared to falter.
Another asset Israel could lose in a peace-collapse would be its new economic prosperity, economists say.

The peace process as such did not trigger the post-Gulf War boom in Israel but it did create a climate of confidence and the promise of stability beloved by foreign investors. The real motor of growth was mass immigration from the former Soviet Union.

"The questions now are, will political unrest deter further immigration, and will it distract the government from tackling the major structural reforms that the Israeli economy needs?" asked economic commentator Pinchas Landau.
"Neither side can afford to go back to their people from these negotiations speaking of failure and deadlock," said Palestinian legislator Ziad Abu Amr.
"We have seen in the past two weeks what the alternative is," he said.
